title: Game & Watch and the bored commuter
hook: Nintendo's first handheld games began with a man idly pressing a calculator on a train.
peek: Gunpei Yokoi saw a bored businessman on a Japanese bullet train fiddling with an LCD calculator to pass the time. It gave him the idea for Game & Watch, small pocket games that also told the time, launched by Nintendo in 1980.
lede: Gunpei Yokoi was a Nintendo engineer who had already made toys such as the Ultra Hand. In the late 1970s, riding a bullet train, he noticed a businessman passing the time by playing with an LCD calculator. Yokoi wondered if a small game could do the same job. The result was Game & Watch, first sold in 1980.

bullets.text: Game & Watch used cheap, low-power LCD screens and chips built for pocket calculators. Each unit played one game, its characters printed into the screen in fixed positions.
Every unit also worked as a clock, and many had an alarm, which is where the name came from. The time showed on screen whenever no game was being played.
The 1982 Game & Watch version of Donkey Kong introduced Yokoi's cross-shaped direction pad. Nintendo patented it and carried it over to its home console controllers.
Yokoi's thinking, often summed up as lateral thinking with withered technology, meant using old, cheap, well-understood parts in new ways. He later led the team behind the Game Boy.
